title: A third of the evening's internet
teaches: Content delivery networks, caching at the edge, adaptive bitrate video, filling caches off-peak, and the cost of moving bytes

blocks.text: In June 2012 Netflix announced Open Connect, its own network for delivering video. Instead of paying other companies to carry its films, Netflix built servers packed with disks, gave them free of charge to internet service providers (ISPs) to install inside their own networks, and placed more at the exchange points where networks interconnect. Each server held the films that local subscribers were likely to watch, so most of an evening's video traffic travelled only a few miles from a rack in the provider's building to the homes it served.

Traffic volume drove this decision. By 2011 Sandvine, a company that sells traffic-measuring equipment to providers, reported that Netflix accounted for about a third of all downstream internet traffic in North America during the evening peak.[^sandvine] An HD stream runs at about 5 Mb/s. A million simultaneous viewers require 5 Tb/s of throughput, a load a large provider can see at 9 p.m. A two-hour film streamed at 5 Mb/s transfers 4.5 GB of data.

Netflix's engineers had to **count the cost** of network routing and egress bandwidth. An hour of video at 5 Mb/s is 2.25 GB. If subscribers watch 100 million hours a day, serving that video from a cloud region at $0.02 per gigabyte transfers 225 petabytes and costs about $4.5 million a day. That figure excludes the cost of carrying the traffic across long-distance links between the cloud and the viewer, which must be provisioned for the evening peak and sit mostly idle at 4 a.m. The engineering problem is to route those bytes over the shortest path during off-peak hours.

Netflix did not invent this architecture. In 1998 MIT mathematician Tom Leighton and his graduate student Danny Lewin founded Akamai using the consistent hashing algorithm they had published the year before (lesson 5), which distributes popular web content across thousands of caching servers located inside many networks.[^lewin] A **content delivery network** (CDN) places servers near users, stores copies of popular content on each server, and routes each user to a nearby server, usually by answering a DNS lookup with that server's IP address. The content owner operates the **origin** server, which stores the complete catalogue. When a CDN server receives a request for an uncached file, it fetches the file from the origin and stores a local copy. This mechanism is **pull-through** caching, which is lesson 5's cache-aside pattern executed by the cache itself.

Data transfer costs depend on which network boundaries the traffic crosses. Cloud providers charge an egress fee of a few cents per gigabyte for data leaving their regions. A network that buys **transit** (the ability to reach the rest of the internet through a larger upstream provider) usually pays per megabit per second of its peak throughput, measured at the 95th percentile of each month's five-minute samples.[^p95] Two networks that exchange roughly equal volumes of traffic often **peer**, connecting directly without charging each other. Hosting an appliance inside the ISP's own network costs the ISP rack space and power, but eliminates transit fees for that traffic because the bytes never cross an external boundary. Data transfer is cheapest when the path is shortest.

An edge server cannot store the entire catalogue; a video library encoded at a dozen bitrates per title requires petabytes of storage. However, full storage is unnecessary because viewing demand is skewed. New series and recent hits account for a large share of total streams, while the thousandth most popular film receives very few requests. In a common model that matches many real catalogues, the title at popularity rank *k* is requested in proportion to 1/*k*: the second most popular title is watched half as much as the first, and the hundredth title is watched one-hundredth as much. This pattern is a **Zipf** distribution.

blocks.caption: A catalogue of 10,000 titles whose popularity falls off as 1/rank to a power s, and an edge cache holding the most popular. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Guess, then find the cache size that serves 90% of views with s at 1.0

blocks.text: Caching 10% of the catalogue serves about 75% of all requests. Serving 90% of requests requires caching well over a third of the catalogue, and serving the final few percentage points requires storing nearly all of it. Doubling the cache capacity yields diminishing returns because of the **long tail** of unpopular titles, which are rarely requested individually but represent a significant fraction of traffic in aggregate. A steeper popularity curve (a larger exponent *s*) increases the hit ratio of a small cache, whereas a flatter curve reduces the hit ratio for any cache size. Because of this distribution, engineers build CDNs in **tiers**: small, fast caches closest to users store the most popular titles, larger caches at exchange points or regional hubs store a wider selection from the tail, and only requests for the rarest titles travel all the way to the origin.

Pull-through caching introduces two problems for video delivery. First, the initial viewer of a title in a local area experiences higher startup latency while the edge server fetches the file from a distant origin. Second, that upstream fetch occurs at the moment of demand, which for residential video is the evening peak when the ISP's external transit links are most congested.

Unlike general-purpose CDNs, Netflix controls its entire catalogue and can forecast regional demand for the next day based on new releases, recent viewing trends, and user demographics. Consequently, Open Connect appliances do not rely solely on pull-through caching. Each night, control-plane software in the cloud calculates which files each appliance should store. The appliances download those files during an overnight **fill window** when network links are mostly idle, allowing ISPs that pay for transit at the 95th percentile to import the data at no additional transit cost. During the evening peak, the appliance serves the pre-loaded files from local storage. This technique is called **pre-positioning**, and it replaces peak-hour cache misses with an offline forecasting calculation. The duration of the fill window dictates the required ingest throughput: an appliance downloading 20 TB of new video over six hours requires 20 × 10¹² × 8 bits / 21,600 s, or about 7.4 Gb/s. Engineers evaluate the forecasting model by measuring the appliance's hit ratio, which is the percentage of evening bytes served from local disk rather than fetched over the network.

Netflix designed the appliances to maximise egress throughput per server. By 2017, Netflix engineers were serving about 100 Gb/s from a single appliance. In 2021, they demonstrated a single FreeBSD server delivering 400 Gb/s of TLS-encrypted video by offloading encryption into the operating system kernel, allowing file data to move from disk to the network interface card without copying bytes into user-space memory.[^ktls] At 5 Mb/s per stream, one 400 Gb/s server can support about 80,000 concurrent viewers.

Netflix kept its control plane in the cloud: user authentication, catalogue browsing, recommendations, appliance selection, and nightly fill calculations all run in AWS regions (using the microservice architecture from lesson 18). Only the video segments are served from the edge appliances. This architecture applies the control plane and data plane separation from lesson 6 at a continental scale, centralising complex state management while routing high-volume video data over the shortest physical path.

The access network between the ISP and the home has variable throughput. A household's available bandwidth fluctuates from minute to minute as other devices start downloads or as the shared local cable loop becomes congested. A video player that requests a single fixed bitrate either underutilises a fast connection or stalls when throughput drops.

Modern video streaming divides each title into **segments** that are a few seconds long and encodes each segment at multiple bitrates to form an **encoding ladder**. In the early 2010s, Netflix used a fixed ladder ranging from 235 kb/s up to 5,800 kb/s for 1080p video.[^ladder] A manifest file lists the available bitrates and segment URLs. The client player downloads one segment at a time over standard HTTP, selecting a bitrate for each request, and maintains a local **buffer** of downloaded segments awaiting playback. Apple's HTTP Live Streaming (HLS, released in 2009) and the MPEG-DASH standard (published in 2012) both use this design. Because each segment is a static file, any standard HTTP cache or CDN server can deliver video without specialized streaming software.

blocks.caption: A player's buffer when the bandwidth drops for fifty seconds. The adaptive player picks its rung from how full the buffer is, and never above 80% of the bandwidth it last measured. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: With the bandwidth falling to 2 Mb/s or less, find a player that never stalls, and play it through

blocks.text: In the simulation, the fixed-bitrate player continues requesting 5.8 Mb/s segments over a 2 Mb/s connection. Each four-second segment takes nearly twelve seconds to download, which drains the playback buffer and causes repeated stalls. The adaptive bitrate (ABR) player switches to a lower bitrate when throughput drops, preserving its playback buffer, and steps back up to higher bitrates when throughput recovers. The video resolution drops for a minute, but playback continues uninterrupted. Because viewers tolerate temporary resolution drops much better than playback stalls, ABR algorithms prioritise preventing buffer underruns over maximising video resolution. In 2014, Te-Yuan Huang and colleagues at Stanford, in collaboration with Netflix, demonstrated that selecting bitrates primarily based on current buffer occupancy resulted in fewer stalls than relying on throughput estimates alone. The adaptive player in the figure combines both signals: it selects a low bitrate when the buffer is nearly empty and the highest bitrate when the buffer is full, while capping its selection at 80% of the throughput measured during the previous segment download.

Netflix built its own CDN because it generated a third of peak evening traffic, controlled a single predictable catalogue, and served workloads suited to caching: large, immutable files read sequentially. Most companies do not meet these criteria and rent capacity from commercial CDNs instead. A website transferring a few hundred terabytes a month can pay a commercial CDN per gigabyte. The build-versus-buy decision comes down to throughput and cost. A few hundred terabytes a month averages less than 1 Gb/s of throughput, which does not justify deploying dedicated hardware. By contrast, an Open Connect appliance serving 40 Gb/s during the evening peak saves the host ISP 40 Gb/s of upstream transit. Assuming a transit price of $0.50 per Mb/s per month, a single appliance saves $20,000 a month in transit fees, which offsets the amortised hardware cost, rack space, power, and operational staffing. Meanwhile, platforms hosting user-generated content, such as YouTube, cannot reliably predict regional demand across millions of new uploads; they rely on pull-through caching for the long tail and pre-position only the most popular videos.

These caching principles apply to any system with a skewed popularity distribution and geographically distributed users, including map tiles (covered in the next lesson), operating system updates, game downloads, and static web assets. Engineers identify the most frequently requested objects, cache them near the users, and replicate them during off-peak hours.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on moving bytes cheaply
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: An edge cache holding the most popular 10% of a catalogue serves 76% of views. Doubling it to 20% raises that to about 84%. Why so little?
choices: Popularity falls steeply, so each extra title added is watched less than the one before it: the long tail
The cache's disks get slower as they fill, so the extra titles are served too slowly to count as hits
Viewers in a neighbourhood watch the same titles, so a bigger cache only stores more copies of them
items.why: Under a Zipf distribution with exponent s = 1, the cumulative share of views grows proportionally to the logarithm of the cache size. The most popular titles provide the largest hit-rate gains, while the long tail requires exponentially more storage for each additional percentage point.

items.ask: Why did Netflix fill its edge appliances in the early morning rather than when viewers asked?
choices: Providers allow appliances to fetch only outside their evening peak, under the terms on which they host them in their racks
Links are nearly idle then, and off-peak transit costs nothing extra, while a miss at 9 p.m. adds to the billed peak
Fills check each file against the origin, which needs disks that are not busy serving
items.why: Networks are provisioned and billed based on peak throughput. Transferring data during off-peak hours incurs no additional transit charges, and pre-positioning files ensures that evening streams do not traverse the provider's external transit links.

items.ask: A video player's buffer is falling fast and holds only six seconds. What should an adaptive player do with the next segment?
choices: Keep the current bitrate, since changing quality in the middle of a scene is what viewers most dislike
Pause playback until the buffer is full again, then carry on at the bitrate it was using before
Fetch it at a lower bitrate, so it arrives in less time than it plays and the buffer stops draining
items.why: A segment encoded at a bitrate lower than the available network throughput downloads faster than real-time playback. Because viewers find playback stalls much more disruptive than temporary drops in resolution, the player prioritises maintaining the buffer.

items.ask: A service streams 100 million hours of video a day at 5 Mb/s straight from a cloud region at 2 cents a gigabyte. Roughly what does the data cost?
choices: About $36 million a day
About $560,000 a day
About $4.5 million a day
items.why: An hour of video at 5 Mb/s is 5 × 10⁶ bits/s × 3,600 s / 8 bits/byte = 2.25 GB. Streaming 100 million hours transfers 225 million GB, which at $0.02 per GB costs $4.5 million a day. Failing to divide bits by 8 yields the incorrect $36 million figure.

items.ask: A site hosts videos uploaded by its users, and most are watched a handful of times. Which way of filling its CDN suits most of its catalogue?
choices: Pull-through caching, since it cannot predict which uploads will be watched where
Pre-positioning every new upload on every edge server overnight, before anyone asks for it
Serving every video from the origin, since caching is of no use to a catalogue with a long tail
items.why: Pre-positioning requires predictable demand and a bounded catalogue. A long tail of user uploads must be fetched from the origin on demand via pull-through caching, while popular uploads at the head of the distribution still benefit from edge caching.

items.ask: Why is streaming video split into segments of a few seconds, each encoded at several bitrates?
choices: Short files compress better than long ones, so the whole film takes less space on the servers
The player switches quality every few seconds as bandwidth changes, and each segment is a file any HTTP cache can hold
Each segment can be sent from a different origin datacentre, so a film never depends on any single datacentre staying up
items.why: Splitting video into segments allows the client player to adjust bitrate dynamically, and serving segments as standard HTTP files allows them to be stored by ordinary web caches and CDNs.

items.ask: Netflix ran sign-in, browsing and recommendations in a cloud region, and served video from appliances inside internet providers. What principle does that split follow?
choices: Keep each customer's data in the country where they live, as data protection rules require
Put the newest software nearest the users, so that bugs show up quickly where they can be seen
Keep the small, complex control decisions in one place, and send the heavy data by the shortest path
items.why: This architecture separates the control plane from the data plane, just like the Google File System (lesson 6): control requests are small and stateful, whereas video transfers are large and benefit from short network paths.

summary: **Calculate data transfer volumes.** At 5 Mb/s, an hour of video is 2.25 GB, so streaming 100 million hours a day transfers 225 petabytes.

**Short network paths minimise transfer costs.** Cloud egress is billed per gigabyte and upstream transit is billed by peak throughput, whereas traffic served from inside an ISP's own network avoids external transit fees.
**A CDN caches content near users.** Edge servers deployed across many networks store popular files, DNS or HTTP routing directs each user to a nearby server, and cache misses fetch from the origin.

**Content popularity follows a steep distribution with a long tail.** Caching 10% of a catalogue can serve 75% of requests, while each subsequent doubling of cache capacity yields smaller hit-rate gains.
**Pre-position content during off-peak hours.** Downloading predicted titles into edge caches overnight shifts cache-fill traffic out of the billed evening peak.

**Centralise the control plane and distribute the data plane.** Netflix executed stateful application logic in the cloud while streaming high-volume video bytes from edge appliances inside ISP networks.

**Adaptive bitrate streaming prevents playback stalls.** Encoding video into multi-second segments across a ladder of bitrates allows the client player to reduce resolution when throughput drops rather than draining its buffer.

**Building a dedicated CDN requires massive scale, a predictable catalogue, and cache-friendly files.** Netflix met all three conditions, whereas most services lack at least one and rent commercial CDN capacity instead.

sandvine.title: Measuring a third
sandvine.text: Sandvine's reports aggregated measurements from deep-packet inspection equipment deployed at partner ISPs. Its estimates for Netflix's share of North American peak downstream traffic rose from roughly 30% in 2011 to over 35% by 2015. These figures represent a sample of participating networks rather than a complete census.

lewin.title: Danny Lewin
lewin.text: Lewin, Akamai's co-founder and chief technology officer, was a passenger on American Airlines Flight 11 on 11 September 2001 and was killed during the hijacking before the plane was flown into the World Trade Center. He was 31.

p95.title: The 95th percentile
p95.text: To calculate 95th-percentile billing, the upstream provider samples traffic throughput every five minutes over a month, discards the highest 5% of samples (about 36 hours of traffic), and bills based on the highest remaining sample. Brief traffic spikes do not increase the bill; sustained evening peak traffic determines the monthly cost, while traffic transferred at 4 a.m. adds nothing.

ktls.title: Encryption in the kernel
ktls.text: Serving HTTPS normally requires reading file data from the kernel into user-space memory, encrypting it within the application process, and writing the ciphertext back to the kernel's network stack. By performing TLS encryption directly inside the kernel (using kTLS) or offloading it to the network interface card, the operating system can transfer data straight from the page cache to the network card via sendfile, similar to the zero-copy mechanism used by Kafka in lesson 16.

ladder.title: A ladder per title
ladder.text: In December 2015, Netflix replaced its fixed encoding ladder with per-title encoding optimisation. Because animation with flat colours compresses much more efficiently than a grainy action film, Netflix generated a custom bitrate ladder for each video based on its visual complexity, reducing bandwidth consumption on simple scenes and improving visual quality on complex ones.
